Question: I'm learning Chinese, but the vocabulary is quite complex. What methods can help me learn them?
Answer: To be honest? I think you are making this difficult for yourself. You say the vocabulary is complex. In what way? I don’t know what your native language is. My native language is English, so for me, French and Russian vocabulary were easier to pick up because the languages are related. Automobile, automobile, автомобиль; theater, théâtre, театр, yeah, that’s easy to see, then you get 汽車 and 戲院 or maybe 劇場. Since the languages are so much different, there aren’t a lot of footholds. But in general, English vocabulary is much more complex, with all the fine distinctions: walk, saunter, stroll, tramp, amble, strut, stride, trudge, and so forth. In general, Chinese vocabulary is more encompassing. Of course there are exceptions, such as the English president could be 總統、會長、社長 or whatever, depending on what the organization the president leads is. And that is the beauty of Chinese vocabulary: 長 means leader, so 會長 is the leader of 會 an association, very often not a profit making corporation; 社長 is generally the president of a 社 a club or something. You just have to add 長 and there’s your leader. BTW, here I am discussing only accumulating vocabulary, not writing. So to build your vocabulary, recite each word or phrase out loud in a loud clear voice twenty times: 社長! 社長! 社長 club president 社長! 社長! and so forth. Try to make a few simple sentences with your phrase, say them out loud. If you know a 社長, try to visualize that person and connect the vocabulary with the image. Repeat for three days and you should have the word down pat. This method works for any language. An important point is, stop telling yourself this is complex, stop telling yourself this is difficult. Relax and enjoy. It does require some persistence and a good pair of lungs, but it’s really not difficult. 加油！

Question: What are the most difficult things to translate?
Answer: The question is a bit vague: things. What does things mean here? If you are asking about vocabulary, it is probably words that are embedded in a particular culture that are hardest to translate; without the context, the words are hard to understand. When I was learning Chinese, I struggled with 義 yì. Righteous? Meaning? Upright? Fair, fake, adopted, even handed? None of the many definitions seemed to fit. A look at the Small Curly etymology of the character didn’t help much: I am a goat? It took me decades to understand how Confucius used the word: the best choice for you at this particular moment, in this particular situation; it is infinitely fluid. In ways, it is similar to C G Jung’s synchronicity. When I started college (National Taiwan Normal U), I was the first and only Westerner enrolled in the undergraduate programs. I tried to explain the American idea of privacy to my friends, with little success. It just didn’t make sense to them. There was no word for it in Chinese, or at least, not any word that my friends knew. Chinese absorbed from Buddhism the concept of 緣 yúan. The word literally means hem, as on clothing. It is the web we weave through our actions that draw in (or do not draw in) others. It is a very important concept and frequently used in common conversation, but very difficult to explain. 我們投緣 literally, we throw yúan, means you hit it off with someone, because in a previous life you had some good connection. Does that help? Many words have a power, a resonance, that is not apparent to those outside the culture. In northern Taiwan, the gaga of the Tayal aborigines is of utmost importance, but how to translate it? It originally meant the rack of firewood drying above the family’s cooking fire. Yeah, that helps. It means the teaching of the ancestors, moral standards, how to behave. It is diluted now, but still powerful. A young lady told me she had to marry her boyfriend soon, because they wanted to live together, but gaga: she didn’t want to risk upsetting the ancestors. The Truku, a related tribe, call it gaya. A few years ago there was a great discussion on Facebook about myna birds, which are not native to Taiwan, but have escaped from their cages and are thriving. A farmer complained that they were eating his millet in the fields, but the myna is black, so gaya. They discussed this for several months, and finally came to the conclusion that mynas are not native to Taiwan, so they are not part of gaya, so go ahead and eat them. So how would you translate those words? In vocabulary, such words are hard to translate. Also sometimes one language takes a particular look at something and has the vocabulary to explain something that is not hard to understand. In Chinese, 口福 kou fu, literally mouth luck, means someone finds good things to eat, happens to get the most delicious food. That’s not hard to understand, but I don’t know of a similar word in English. Beyond vocabulary, poetry is impossible to translate. This could be because translators are usually not poets. I am certainly no poet. I can’t find the link now; a while back on Quora, I literally translated a Chinese poem; it was like plucking all the feathers from a phoenix. The colors are there, but it’s dead. A Maori poet who doesn’t know Chinese saw the mess I left, and with his poetic talent, produced a magnificent “translation.” In rare circumstances it is possible to translate a pun, but most just die. 我們不投緣。那麼投方，怎樣？We don’t throw yúan. Then throw square, okay? Yuck yuck… Jokes are easy to translate, but the cultural context often makes them unintelligible. Good luck telling American jokes to Chinese audiences. Bob Hope one time was entertaining American servicemen in Japan. Then he thought, ‘I should do something for our hosts,’ so he performed for a Japanese audience, with his interpreter translating into Japanese. The audience roared every time he told a joke. Hope was pleased. After the show, he told the interpreter, ‘That was great! Those jokes usually don’t get such a great response.’ The interpreter said, “No way Japanese people would understand those American jokes, boss. Every time you told the punchline, I told the audience, Mr Hope has told you a joke that Americans think is funny, so please laugh.”

Question: If a word has an equivalent that has the same meaning and has less syllables or fewer letters, why don't we just use the simpler word?
Answer: That is an excellent idea. Winston Churchill, who was a master of prose, said, ‘Short words are best.’ Why? Think of an arrowhead. If you want to penetrate, you want the power focused on one small spot, not spread out. Longer words diffuse the power, and are weaker. Another problem is that longer words are often jargon, bombastic, or pedantic. People used to say a car slid on the road; now they say it hydroplaned. Don’t say you visually examined something; you looked at it. When you choose words, lop off as many suffixes as you can without changing the meaning; write with verbs, nouns, and then adjectives and adverbs. Don’t use supportive; support serves your purpose. Don’t say make an identification; identify. Utilize serves no useful purpose but to mark the author as a pedant or sloppy writer. Use use. Do not finalize; finish or end. You do sometimes want a longer word, for the rhythm of your sentences. This requires you read and practice a lot, to tune your ear. In short, try not to write like a lawyer or a professor. Lawyers are obliged to close up all possible loopholes. Professors love to obfuscate (see? sometimes you do want to use longer words). Neither is a good model for writing well.

Question: How did people learn a new language without technology?
Answer: First, let’s talk about what you mean by technology. When anthropologists discuss technology, they mean “fashioning implements, practicing manual arts and skills, and extracting or collecting materials.” In that sense, technology is older than our species, and may even be older than language. So when you ask about technology, I guess you are talking about stuff with a lot electronics and transistors. But it’s wise to use words carefully. Language communicates by using words appropriately. There were some people in Western schools who learned Greek and Latin by memorizing grammar and vocabulary, but they were not expected to go out and order bubble tea with their new language. People generally learned languages only when they needed them. They needed them because they needed to talk to people, for whatever reason. Listen, repeat, imitate, make mistakes, find out what’s wrong, talk some more, make some more mistakes, repeat, listen, and gradually get the hang of it. In brutal early centuries, people were kidnapped from Africa and sold into slavery in Europe, Arabia, and the Americas. Contemporary records show that from the first time the poor enslaved person heard a language, they could speak well enough within about three months. Being illiterate and having no access to modern technology was a great help in their progress. They were “encouraged” to work on their language with whippings and beatings, but they could use the language well enough within about three months. This bears out with my own experience learning Mandarin, and fortunately nobody whipped me. I have heard other people discussing learning languages this way, and three or four months seems about right. Of course at this level you are still making a lot of mistakes and misunderstanding, or simply not understanding a lot of what you hear, but you have already achieved basic competency. A lot of workers come to Taiwan from Indonesia, Thailand, the Philippines, and Viet Nam, and usually by about three months they have a good grasp of Mandarin. I have met some foreign workers who spoke Mandarin very fluently, with little or no accent, within about a year. This is probably because first, they are highly motivated because their occupation relies on it. Second, they are not learning in an academic setting where you told it will take you years and years to learn a language, and they do not see their papers marked in red. In The Innocent Anthropologist: Notes from a Mud Hut, Nigel Barley tells about finishing his studies in anthropology in Cambridge and Oxford and going to Cameroon to do some real anthropology, living in a local village. After he had been there about two weeks, the locals decided that he must be pretty stupid, because he had been there all of two weeks and still couldn’t speak their language. Obviously they didn’t expect him to discuss literature or astronomy in their language, but they expected that by two weeks he should have been able to carry on a basic conversation. This is because they learned languages without academic theory and without modern technology.

Question: How common is the use of alliteration in Chinese poetry?
Answer: Alliterations are not that common in Chinese poetry. In roughly the 3rd or 4th century ce, they started setting forms for poetry. By the Tang, say around the 7th century ce, set forms were usually used: so many words in each line, with the tones for each position established (平仄), and the rhyming pattern set. Also, I’d like to point out that, especially since about the 3rd century, poems are mercifully brief. You don’t get those monsters (as in English poetry) that go on for pages and pages. You can have a complete, polished poem in twenty syllables. It’s not easy! (Before that, especially during the Han and a while after, they had a form of poetry called 賦 fu, that does go on for pages. Fu used especially ornate vocabulary. My theory is that in the Han, to be an official, you had to memorize 9,000 characters, so if you’ve memorized them, you may as well use them. In Chinese, they have a special beauty, from the forms of the characters. I don’t think there’s any way to translate it. Aside: everybody celebrates Double Fifth but nobody really pays much attention to old Ch’ü/Qu Yuan from about 300bce and his works, so every Double Fifth, I chant his great poem 離騷 Li Sao. It takes about half an hour, so you can see it is quite long. But later poetry was much shorter.) Poetry is not my focus, but I can’t really think of any famous poems that use alliteration.

Question: Which country has a longer history, China or Japan?
Answer: To avoid argument, let’s first talk about what you mean by history. If I recall correctly, Japan was originally attached to the Eurasian plate and about 15 million years ago, formed into separate islands. So in that sense, China and Japan probably have equally long histories. (An interesting aside is that this ancient process is still going on. In that humongous earthquake a few years ago, it seems the entire nation moved east about nine meters!) If you mean written history, then definitely China. Chinese writing was mature by 3300 years ago, give or take a few months. Japan had no writing until they started learning how to write Chinese about 1500 years ago. China has documents that go back to the Neolithic, before the advent of writing, that were orally transmitted for generations. That will take you back a good 4,000 years, long before anything Japanese. If you are asking about the cultures, then you can trace a direct line in artifacts back 8,000 years in China. But ultimately, this question is useless. The only possible reason I can imagine anyone would be interested in which country had a longer history is a college student trying to decide whether to sign up for Chinese History 101 or Japanese History 101 ~ which country has the shorter history? sign up for that one so you don’t have so much material to ingest.

Question: What should my Chinese character name be like? My European-Belgian name is Michail Verschuere. Michael is named after the archangel that killed the dragon in the Bible. The family name is "from a barn". I was adviced to use 米海游 费舍尔 .
Answer: That is a transliteration, Mihaiyou Feisheer, and immediately marks you as a foreigner who doesn’t use Chinese much. The only people with six words in their names are (were) Manchu emperors or indigenous Taiwanese whose Austronesian names don’t fit Chinese patterns. The vast majority of Chinese names are two or three words / syllables. The first is the family name; there is a set of words that can be used as family names. What follows is the given name, and just about anything can be used for a given name. Of course most parents wouldn’t name their kid something like Stupid or Ugly, but you may use any word you like for a name. Some words are rarely used in names, like 爾/尔, but that doesn’t mean you can’t use them. Just a bit odd. Here is not the place to go into the ins and outs of Chinese names, such as generation markers. How much do you want your Chinese name to sound like your European name? You could use either 米 or 費 for a family name. 米 is quicker to write, and 費 also means expenses, charges, but you could choose either one. Okay, barn, 倉 would be like a barn, but don’t use 米倉! That’s naming yourself a silo for rice. If you are a comedian, okay, but otherwise, not so. 費倉 isn’t a whole lot better. Maybe you could use 藏, a similar sound, means to hold, to contain, to treasure. But I don’t think that works very well with either of those surnames. Would you consider using something else as a surname? If you really like sailing or surfing, you could use 海游 for a name, (ocean swimming), but it sounds a bit silly. Anyway, I think it would be better to find a name that fits you, fits your interests or proclivities or wishes, than stick to the original sounds, because there are no final Ls in Chinese, or a V sound in Mandarin. I’d say, think about this, don’t rush it, find a good name for yourself. BTW, you won’t get any points for killing dragons in Chinese cultural areas! Dragons are esteemed, even beloved; they bring rain and blessings.

Question: Do you believe that religions are “man-made”? Why?
Answer: For the moment, we won’t worry about what a “religion” is. Ultimately, all religions are “man-made” because they have to fit into our stubborn little brains. We try to reduce things to words and concepts, so we pare and trim and tailor vast ideas so we can grasp them. As a Buddhist, obviously I worship no gods or buddhas. But I know that our understanding is limited and primitive, a convenience to help us on our way. It’s like teaching astrophysics to little kids: first you start with easy ideas that they can grasp, and as their understanding increases, you expand the information, and even sometimes crack apart their earlier ideas. If a second grader has to imagine someone walking across the surface of Jupiter, good enough for the time being; sooner or later you can teach them that Jupiter is a gas giant with no surface. First establish the ideas, then tune them. Consider the bodhisattva Samantabhadra/普賢菩薩, who is often depicted riding an elephant with six tusks. I have long suspected that the real bodhisattva is the elephant, and the human figure is just a bauble for us to fix our attention on. Buddhism doesn’t worry about “truth” because there are so many facets and so many levels. Certainly you don’t suppose that your dog views your home the same way you do, or that an octopus or dolphin has the same concepts of the ocean that we do. Take it one step at a time. As we are now equipped with human brains, we process man-made information more easily, so religions are in that sense man-made.
